events.title: Washington's oldest rocks: the Belt Supergroup
events.summary: The oldest rocks you can touch in Washington are mudstones, sandstones and limy layers of the Belt Supergroup in the state's far northeast corner (Pend Oreille and Stevens counties, Colville National Forest). They settled in a vast, shallow inland basin on the ancient continent of Laurentia when the only life was microbial; stromatolite mounds built by cyanobacteria are preserved in them. Some ten miles of these sediments bury an even older continental basement that never reaches the surface in Washington; rocks of about 2.5 billion years crop out just across the Idaho line. (A 2024 USGS field guide argues some strata mapped as Belt are younger; 1.47-1.40 billion years remains the standard public figure.)
events.at_your_spot: {place} sits over continental crust that was already old when these rocks formed; the nearest Belt Supergroup outcrops are in Pend Oreille and Stevens counties, about {distance} away.

events.title: Rodinia breaks apart: North America's new western edge
events.summary: When the supercontinent Rodinia rifted apart, the piece that became North America was left with a brand-new western coastline running roughly through today's northeastern Washington. Rift-valley gravels and glacial debris of the Windermere Group (about 700 million years old) record that break-up and a global 'Snowball Earth' cold spell. Everything west of this line, most of the state, did not exist yet; it would arrive piece by piece over the next half-billion years.

events.title: Warm Cambrian seas: the Metaline limestone and Gardner Cave
events.summary: Northeastern Washington was the continental shelf of North America, under a warm shallow sea where shells and reef debris piled up into more than 3,000 feet of Metaline limestone, capped by black Ordovician slate. Trilobites and graptolites are its fossils. That limestone later hosted the Pend Oreille zinc-lead mines and, dissolved by rainwater, Gardner Cave, one of Washington's longest limestone caves (State Parks ranks it third), about 1,055 feet long with the first 494 feet open on guided tours, in Crawford State Park near Metaline Falls.
events.at_your_spot: In the Cambrian the shoreline of North America lay near present-day Metaline Falls; {place} was either on that shelf or far out to sea.

events.title: Island arcs dock: Quesnellia and the Okanogan Highlands
events.summary: The first big piece of 'new' Washington arrived in the Jurassic: Quesnellia, a volcanic island arc that had been growing offshore since the Mississippian, was shoved onto the old continental edge. The collision squeezed and lifted the Kootenay Arc (about 160 million years ago) and set the stage for huge granite bodies such as the Cretaceous Okanogan Batholith. Much later, in the Eocene (56-34 million years ago), the crust here stretched and the Okanogan and Kettle dome-and-basin landscape formed.

events.title: The North Cascades, Methow and San Juan terranes are welded on
events.when: about 100 to 84 million years ago (mid-Late Cretaceous), building on Jurassic pieces
events.summary: Long-running subduction dragged a jumble of exotic crust (ocean floor, island arcs, deep-sea sediments) against the continent. The San Juan Islands and the Northwest Cascades are stacked thrust sheets of such terranes, pinned down before about 84 million years ago by the overlying Nanaimo Group sediments; the Methow Valley records island-arc and ocean-floor terranes docking in the middle and late Cretaceous; and the North Cascades crystalline core was cooked and squeezed at depth into the gneisses seen at Stehekin and Washington Pass. Paleomagnetic data suggest some of these blocks formed up to a thousand miles to the south and slid north along the coast.

events.title: Siletzia: a volcanic ocean plateau collides and becomes western Washington's basement
events.when: eruptions 56-48 million years ago; collision 51-50 million years ago (early Eocene)
events.summary: An enormous pile of submarine basalt, Siletzia, possibly built over the young Yellowstone hotspot, rode in on the Farallon plate and jammed against North America about 51-50 million years ago, too thick to subduct. Its Washington part is the Crescent Formation: pillow lavas that now form the horseshoe of ridges around the Olympic Mountains (Hurricane Ridge road cuts), the Black Hills and Willapa Hills, and the hidden basement beneath Seattle, Tacoma and the whole Puget Lowland. The collision ended the old coastline, folded the Chuckanut and Swauk basins, and reset the subduction zone to roughly its present position.
events.at_your_spot: Deep beneath {place}, the basement rock is Siletzia/Crescent Formation basalt: sea-floor volcanoes that docked here about 50 million years ago.

events.title: Eocene palm forests and coal swamps: Chuckanut, Swauk and the Puget Group
events.when: about 57 to 38 million years ago (late Paleocene to late Eocene)
events.summary: Western Washington was a steamy, subtropical river plain. Fan palms, tree ferns and swamp cypresses grew along braided rivers that laid down the Chuckanut Formation around Bellingham (fossil palm fronds and the tracks of the giant flightless bird Diatryma at Racehorse Creek), the Swauk Formation near Blewett Pass, and later the Puget Group of the Seattle area. Peat from those swamps became the coal that built Newcastle, Renton, Black Diamond, Issaquah and Roslyn in the 1800s. Cooling late in the Eocene drove the palms out for good.
events.at_your_spot: About 50 million years ago {place} was a hot, humid river floodplain with palms and tree ferns; the coal under the Eastside and the Cle Elum valley is the remains of those swamps.

events.title: Stonerose: the Republic fossil lake
events.summary: As the crust of the Okanogan Highlands stretched apart (53-45 million years ago), a deep upland lake filled the Republic graben. Its fine lakebed shales, the Klondike Mountain Formation, dated 49.4 +/- 0.5 million years, preserve one of the world's finest Eocene floras: dawn redwood, sassafras, early relatives of roses, maples and apples, plus insects, fish and feathers. At the Stonerose Interpretive Center in Republic, visitors can dig their own fossils (important finds stay in the research collection; the Burke Museum holds a major collection too).

events.title: The Cascade volcanic arc switches on
events.when: about 40-37 million years ago, and still active
events.summary: Once Siletzia had reset the plate boundary, the sinking ocean plate began feeding magma to a new line of volcanoes, the ancestral Cascades, starting about 40-37 million years ago (DNR gives 43-37). Early vents punched through shallow seas and coastal plains in southwest Washington; their ash and lava (the Ohanapecosh and Stevens Ridge formations) make up the foundations of Mount Rainier National Park. The volcanoes we see today are only the newest instalments of this 40-million-year arc.

events.title: Columbia River Basalt floods bury a third of Washington
events.when: about 16.7 to 6 million years ago (Miocene); more than 95% erupted 16.7-15.9 Ma
events.summary: From fissures in southeast Washington and adjacent Oregon and Idaho, probably fed by the Yellowstone hotspot, more than 300 floods of basalt lava poured out, each filling the landscape like water in a basin; more than 95% of it erupted in well under a million years, between about 16.7 and 15.9 million years ago (Kasbohm & Schoene 2018). The flows cover over 80,000 square miles across three states and about 36% of Washington: everything from Spokane, Pullman, Walla Walla and the Tri-Cities to Yakima, Moses Lake, Wenatchee's east side and Goldendale, stacked up to two miles thick under the Pasco Basin. Some flows ran down the Columbia River Gorge to Vancouver and all the way to the Pacific. The Puget Lowland, Olympics, North Cascades and the northeast highlands were never buried. Later folding of the cooled basalt made the Yakima ridges.

events.title: Ginkgo Petrified Forest at Vantage
events.summary: Between basalt floods, a lake and swampy forest grew where the Columbia now cuts through at Vantage. When the next lava (the Ginkgo flow of the Wanapum Basalt) poured in, waterlogged logs (ginkgo, Douglas-fir, spruce, elm, sweetgum, walnut and more than 50 species in all) were sealed under lava and slowly turned to stone. George Beck of Ellensburg recognized the deposit in the 1930s; it is now Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park, and petrified wood is Washington's state gem.

events.title: The Blue Lake Rhino
events.when: about 15 million years ago (middle Miocene); discovered July 1935
events.summary: A rhinoceros (Diceratherium) lying dead in a shallow lake was engulfed by a basalt flow; the water chilled the lava into pillows around the carcass and left a rhino-shaped cavity in the rock. In July 1935 fossil hunters scrambling along the cliffs of Jasper Canyon at the east end of Blue Lake, in the lower Grand Coulee, found the cave with bone fragments and a jaw inside. A cast of the cavity is displayed at the Burke Museum; the cave itself is a strenuous, unmarked scramble in Sun Lakes-Dry Falls State Park.

events.title: The Olympic Mountains rise from the sea
events.when: wedge building since ~45 Ma; land emerges about 18-13 million years ago; still rising
events.summary: The Olympics are not volcanoes: they are deep-sea sandstones and shales scraped off the sinking Juan de Fuca plate and stuffed under the rim of Siletzia basalt, then squeezed upward. Sediment studies show the peninsula first broke the sea surface about 16.5-13 million years ago (DNR says the rise began around 18 Ma), and the range has been lifting, and eroding just as fast, ever since. The Hurricane Ridge fault is the seam between the core sandstones and the basalt rim; Mount Olympus (7,980 ft) is the high point.
events.at_your_spot: {place} looks toward the Olympics, a pile of sea-floor sediment that has been shoved up out of the Pacific for the last 15 million years or so.

events.title: The Cascade Range is lifted to its modern height
events.when: roughly 12 to 4 million years ago (late Miocene-Pliocene)
events.summary: For most of their history the Cascades were a belt of volcanoes on low ground, with lavas and ash spilling east onto the basalt plateau. Then the whole range was pushed up as a block: rock-cooling studies show rapid uplift and erosion in Washington 12-8 million years ago, and the Burke Museum's (archived 2002) summary places the final rise of the modern range at 5-7 million years ago. The rain shadow that makes eastern Washington dry, and the river canyons that cut the range, date from this time.

events.title: The modern volcanoes are born: Adams, Rainier, St. Helens, Baker
events.when: about 520,000 to 140,000 years ago (and still active)
events.summary: The peaks on today's skyline are young. Mount Adams (Pahto to the Yakama) began erupting about 520,000 years ago; the present Mount Rainier (Tahoma, Təqʷuʔməʔ) started building about 500,000 years ago on the stump of an older volcano; Mount St. Helens' (Lawetlat'la, Loowit) first eruptions date to about 300,000 years ago, though its graceful pre-1980 cone was less than 3,000 years old; and Mount Baker (Kulshan) began around 140,000 years ago, with most of its cone built 40,000-12,000 years ago. Glacier Peak (Dakobed) is likewise older than the last ice age. All five are considered active.
events.at_your_spot: From {place}, {nearest_volcano} ({distance} away) is geologically brand new: it has been building for only the last few hundred thousand years, and it is still active.

events.title: Earlier ice ages: the Double Bluff and Possession glaciations
events.summary: The Vashon ice was only the latest of several Cordilleran ice sheets to fill the Puget Lowland. Sea cliffs on Whidbey Island (Double Bluff, Possession Point) expose older glacial deposits from about 190,000-125,000 and 80,000-60,000 years ago, separated by warm-interval river, lake and peat beds (the Whidbey Formation and the Olympia beds, which are well exposed at the base of the Discovery Park bluffs in Seattle, below the Lawton Clay whose type section is there). Each ice sheet reshaped the lowland and buried the one before.
events.at_your_spot: The layered bluffs near {place} record at least three ice sheets; the Vashon ice was only the most recent.

events.title: The Okanogan Lobe dams the Columbia: Glacial Lake Columbia, Grand Coulee and Dry Falls
events.summary: East of the Cascades, tongues of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet filled the Okanogan, Methow, Sanpoil, Colville and Pend Oreille valleys. The Okanogan Lobe spread across the Waterville Plateau to the Withrow Moraine and plugged the Columbia River (19,000-17,000 years ago), backing up Glacial Lake Columbia, which lasted until about 14,000 years ago (a few centuries after the last Missoula flood). Missoula floods pouring into that lake were shunted south through Grand Coulee, cutting the 50-mile canyon and the 3.5-mile-wide, 400-foot Dry Falls between about 17,000 and 14,000 years ago. Spokane sat just beyond the ice, under the path of the floods.

events.title: The Missoula floods carve the Channeled Scablands
events.summary: Again and again, at least 75 times before a Mount St. Helens ash fall 16,000 years ago and 30 or more times after, an ice dam in Idaho broke and Glacial Lake Missoula emptied across eastern Washington in days. The floods stripped the Palouse soil off the Cheney-Palouse tract south of Spokane, scoured the Grand Coulee, Moses Coulee and Quincy Basin, and then jammed at Wallula Gap, pooling as temporary Lake Lewis up to about 1,200-1,250 feet above sea level: the Pasco Basin, the Tri-Cities (under some 800 feet of water), the Yakima Valley to near Yakima, the Walla Walla and Touchet valleys, and the Snake valley past Lewiston were all drowned for days to weeks. West of the gorge the water spread across the Portland Basin, putting Vancouver, Camas and Washougal under hundreds of feet of water before it ran on to the sea; the Puget Lowland and the outer coast were untouched.

events.title: The Puget Lobe: the Vashon ice sheet buries Seattle, Tacoma and Olympia
events.when: about 19,000 to 16,000 years ago; maximum about 17,000 years ago
events.summary: A lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet flowed south out of British Columbia, filled the Puget Lowland and reached its limit near Tenino, south of Olympia, about 17,000 years ago. The ice was roughly 5,000 feet thick at Bellingham, about 3,000 feet over Seattle, about 2,000 feet over Tacoma and about 1,000 feet near Olympia. Seattle was under ice for less than 2,000 years, yet the ice left almost everything we see: the north-south ridges of Capitol Hill, Queen Anne and Beacon Hill are glacially streamlined drumlins; the Lawton Clay, Esperance Sand and Vashon till in the Discovery Park bluffs are its deposits; and meltwater under the ice gouged the deep troughs of Puget Sound, Lake Washington and Hood Canal. By about 16,000 years ago the ice front had melted back north of Seattle.

events.title: Glacial Lakes Russell and Bretz: the lowland becomes a lake
events.summary: With the ice plugging the Strait of Juan de Fuca, meltwater could not escape north, so as the glacier advanced and again as it retreated a vast lake filled the lowland south of the ice front. Glacial Lake Russell stretched from the Seattle area to the Black Hills and spilled over the Black Lake divide near Olympia into the Chehalis River and out to Grays Harbor, which is why the Chehalis valley is far too wide for its river. When the ice uncovered Admiralty Inlet, a lower lake, Glacial Lake Bretz, drained north through the Chimacum Valley to Discovery Bay. The lakes' old shorelines and deltas now tilt upward to the north by about a metre per kilometre because the land has rebounded since the ice left.

events.title: Puget Sound is born: the sea floods in and the land rebounds
events.summary: Once the retreating ice opened the Strait, seawater poured into the lowland, floated the remaining ice and dropped shell-bearing glacial-marine mud (the Everson drift of Bellingham, Whidbey and Everett) over the northern and central lowland. The crust had sunk only part way under the ice, about 35-70 percent of the way to full equilibrium under the load (Thorson 1981), and once the ice left it rose quickly; maximum postglacial uplift reached about 140 m in the northern lowland, and the lowland had lifted out of the sea by roughly 13,000 years ago. Puget Sound, Lake Washington and the islands took their modern outlines over the following millennia as sea level rose worldwide.
events.at_your_spot: Not long after the ice left, salt water reached far inland past {place}; the land has since risen tens of metres, leaving old beaches high above today's shore.

events.title: Ice-age giants and the earliest known people: mammoths, mastodons, bison and sloths
events.summary: As the ice and floods receded, Washington was grassland and parkland roamed by Columbian mammoths (the state fossil; one at Coyote Canyon near Kennewick died about 17,000 years ago in Missoula-flood sediments), American mastodons, giant Bison antiquus and Jefferson's ground sloths. Workers digging a light-tower footing at Sea-Tac Airport in 1961 found a ground sloth, radiocarbon-dated to about 12,500-12,700 years (roughly 15,000 calendar years) ago, now mounted at the Burke Museum. On Orcas Island a bison butchered by people about 13,700 years ago (Ayer Pond) and the Manis mastodon at Sequim show that people, ancestors of today's tribes, were hunting here within a thousand years of the ice leaving. Most of these giants were extinct by about 11,000 years ago. The tribes of Washington have lived here since time immemorial; archaeological dates are minimum ages, not arrival dates.

events.title: The Manis mastodon: people hunting at Sequim
events.when: about 13,800 years ago (refined to about 13,900 in 2023); discovered August 8, 1977
events.summary: Digging a pond with a backhoe on his Happy Valley farm near Sequim in 1977, in the traditional territory of the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe, Emanuel Manis turned up mastodon tusks. Washington State University's Carl Gustafson found a rib with a sharpened bone point embedded in it, a spear tip made from another mastodon's bone. Redating and CT scanning in 2011 (Waters et al., Science) put the kill at about 13,800 years ago, refined to about 13,900 in 2023, several centuries before the Clovis culture, making it among the oldest evidence of people anywhere in the Americas and the oldest known trace of people in Washington. The tusks and main bones are displayed at the Sequim Museum & Arts Center; the rib with the point was transferred to the Washington State Historical Society in Tacoma in 2019.

events.title: Glacier Peak's great ash eruptions
events.summary: Washington's most remote volcano produced a burst of six to nine explosive eruptions within a few centuries (USGS counts differ by how the layers are split), the largest throwing out more than five times the tephra of Mount St. Helens in 1980, among the biggest Cascade eruptions since the ice age. Ash drifted east over the whole of eastern Washington and on to Montana and beyond; near Chelan the deposit is more than a foot thick, and the layer lies on top of all the Missoula-flood deposits, which is how geologists know the floods had ended. Glacier Peak has erupted several more times since, most recently about 300 years ago.

events.title: Mazama ash falls across Washington
events.when: about 7,700 years ago (7,682-7,584 calendar years BP)
events.summary: When Mount Mazama in Oregon blew itself apart to create Crater Lake, the biggest eruption in the Cascades in the last 10,000 years, its ash blanketed Washington: an orange-tan layer centimetres thick in eastern-Washington road cuts and thicker toward the Oregon line, and traceable in lake and bog muds even in the Puget Lowland. The layer is a time marker geologists use everywhere in the state: anything beneath it is older than 7,700 years. Klamath oral tradition (southern Oregon) recalls the eruption.

events.title: The Osceola Mudflow: Mount Rainier's summit collapses into the lowland
events.summary: An eruption triggered the collapse of Mount Rainier's weakened, clay-rich summit and northeast flank. About 3.8 cubic kilometres of rock turned into a wall of mud that ran more than 70 miles down the White River, buried the Enumclaw plateau and spread across 212 square miles of lowland, reaching Kent, Auburn, Sumner and an arm of Puget Sound at what is now the Port of Tacoma. It is the largest lahar known from Rainier and lopped some 1,000-2,000 feet off the mountain. Kent, Auburn, Enumclaw, Buckley and much of the Kent valley, homeland of the Muckleshoot and Puyallup peoples, stand on its deposits.
events.at_your_spot: {place} is built on the Osceola Mudflow: the valley floor here was laid down in a single day about 5,600 years ago when Mount Rainier's summit fell into the lowland.

events.title: The Seattle Fault earthquake of 923-924 CE
events.summary: A magnitude 7-7.5 earthquake on the Seattle Fault, the east-west fault under the stadiums, I-90 and Bainbridge Island, lifted Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island about 7 metres (23 feet) and Alki Point about 4 metres (13 feet) out of Puget Sound in an instant, while the ground north of the fault at West Point dropped 1-1.5 metres. A tsunami swept sand across West Point and Cultus Bay; hillsides slid into Lake Washington off Mercer Island and near Saint Edward State Park, carrying whole forests that still stand upright under water; and landslides fell into Lake Sammamish. Tree rings, anchored by a cosmic-ray spike of 774-775 CE recorded in the wood, pin the quake to between the growing seasons of 923 and 924 CE (Black et al. 2023); Coast Salish oral traditions (Suquamish, Duwamish and neighbouring peoples) of a'yahos, the shaking serpent-spirit, are tied to places along the fault (Ludwin et al. 2005). The 2023 study found the Saddle Mountain fault near Hood Canal ruptured at the same time, so the combined event could have reached magnitude 7.8. It is the only time in at least 7,500 years that the Seattle Fault lifted the shoreline by metres; trenches on Bainbridge Island record three or four smaller (about magnitude 7) Seattle Fault quakes between roughly 2,500 and 1,000 years ago.

events.title: The Electron Mudflow buries the Puyallup valley
events.summary: Without any eruption, a slab of rotten, hydrothermally altered rock on Mount Rainier's west face (Sunset Amphitheater) let go and became a clay-rich lahar of about 0.26 cubic kilometres. It was 30 metres deep where it left the mountains at Electron and flowed down the Puyallup valley, the Puyallup Tribe's homeland, at least as far as Sumner, burying the forest and leaving the flat valley floor that Orting now sits on. Tree-ring and radiocarbon work dates it to about 1507 CE, and Indigenous narratives describe it. Because it needed no eruption warning, it is the scenario behind the Puyallup valley's lahar sirens and Orting's evacuation drills.
events.at_your_spot: {place} stands on the Electron Mudflow; about 500 years ago this valley floor was buried under metres of mud from Mount Rainier with no warning, and the sirens here exist because it could happen again.

events.title: The great Cascadia earthquake of January 26, 1700
events.summary: The whole Cascadia subduction zone, some 1,000 km from Vancouver Island to northern California, ruptured in a magnitude ~9 earthquake. The outer coast dropped 1-2 metres in moments, drowning forests in salt water (the ghost cedars of the Copalis River and Willapa Bay died in the winter of 1699-1700 by tree-ring count) and a tsunami tens of feet high swept the coast and, about ten hours later, Japan, where villagers recorded an 'orphan' tsunami with no felt quake. Oral histories of coastal nations, including the Makah, Quileute, Hoh and Quinault, recall the shaking and the waves (Ludwin et al. 2005). Willapa Bay marshes record seven such quakes in 3,500 years and deep-sea turbidites 19 in 10,000 years, averaging about 500 years apart.
events.at_your_spot: On the night of January 26, 1700, {place} shook for several minutes; on the outer coast the land sank and a tsunami followed within half an hour. The next one is a matter of when, not if (see mil.wa.gov for how to prepare).

events.title: The 1872 North Cascades (Chelan-Entiat) earthquake
events.summary: The largest crustal earthquake in Washington's written history, magnitude about 6.5-7.0 (best estimate 6.8), struck near Entiat and the south end of Lake Chelan and was felt from British Columbia to Oregon and Montana. A landslide at Ribbon Cliff dammed the Columbia River for hours, hot springs changed, and settlers and Indigenous residents at Lake Chelan and along the Columbia (ancestors of today's Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation) reported ground cracks and geysering sand. Lidar has since revealed a fresh 1-2 metre scarp on the Spencer Canyon fault southwest of Entiat, the likely source, and the Entiat earthquake cluster still active today may be its aftershocks.

events.title: The 1949 Olympia earthquake
events.summary: A deep (about 50 km) earthquake inside the sinking Juan de Fuca plate, centered between Olympia and Tacoma, shook western Washington at magnitude 7.1 (some modern recalculations give 6.7), the strongest in the region's recorded history. Eight people died, including schoolchildren struck by falling masonry, and dozens were seriously hurt; the Capitol dome in Olympia, downtown Seattle and Tacoma buildings and dozens of schools were damaged. It was the first of three deep 'Benioff' quakes (1949, 1965, 2001) that define the Puget Sound region's most frequent big-earthquake type.
events.at_your_spot: At midday on April 13, 1949, {place} shook hard for about half a minute; brick parapets and chimneys fell across Puget Sound cities.

events.title: The 1965 Seattle-Tacoma earthquake
events.summary: Another deep intraslab quake, magnitude 6.7 (USGS 6.5), struck about 60 km beneath the Des Moines area between Seattle and Tacoma and shook for about 45 seconds. Seven people died (three from falling debris in Pioneer Square and at the Fisher Flouring Mills on Harbor Island, four from heart attacks) and damage reached about $12.5 million in 1965 dollars, with the worst in Seattle's older brick districts and on filled ground.
events.at_your_spot: On the morning of April 29, 1965, {place} rocked for 45 seconds; older brick buildings and chimneys nearby were the casualties.

events.title: Mount St. Helens erupts
events.summary: A magnitude 5.1 earthquake set off the largest landslide in recorded history, uncorking a sideways blast that flattened 230 square miles of forest, followed by a nine-hour ash column 15 miles high and lahars that choked the Toutle and Cowlitz rivers and the Columbia shipping channel. Fifty-seven people died. The ash cloud blacked out Yakima within an hour and Spokane by afternoon, closed I-90 under inches of grit at Ritzville and dusted eleven states; the mountain, sacred to the Cowlitz Tribe and the Yakama Nation as Lawetlat'la, lost 1,300 feet of its summit. Washington's volcanoes went from scenery to hazard overnight, and the Cascades Volcano Observatory was founded to watch them.
events.at_your_spot: On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens, {distance} from {place}, blew out its north side; Yakima went dark by mid-morning and Ritzville was buried under inches of ash.

events.title: The 2001 Nisqually earthquake
events.summary: A magnitude 6.8 quake 52 km beneath the Nisqually delta near Anderson Island shook the Puget Sound region for about 40 seconds. One person died of a heart attack and about 400 were injured; damage of $1-4 billion hit Pioneer Square's brick buildings, the Capitol dome, Sea-Tac's control tower and the Alaskan Way Viaduct, whose cracking led to its replacement by the SR 99 tunnel in 2019. Because it was deep, like 1949 and 1965, shaking was strong but brief; a shallow Seattle Fault quake of the same size would be far worse.
events.at_your_spot: On February 28, 2001, {place} swayed for 40 seconds; many older buildings nearby were retrofitted afterward.

events.title: Today: Washington rides the leading edge of a subduction zone
events.when: the last ~30 million years, and now
events.summary: Offshore, the small Juan de Fuca plate, the last fragment of the ancient Farallon plate, is sliding northeast under Washington at 3-4 cm per year, about half its speed of 7 million years ago. That sinking slab feeds the Cascade volcanoes, flexes the coast, generates slow 'tremor' episodes under Puget Sound every 14 months or so, and stores the strain for magnitude-9 Cascadia earthquakes (last one 1700; average spacing about 500 years). At the same time the Oregon coast block rotates clockwise and squeezes western Washington northward against Canada, loading the shallow Seattle, Tacoma and other crustal faults.
events.at_your_spot: Every year {place} is pushed a few millimetres northeast and squeezed by the plate sinking offshore; the next great Cascadia quake will shake it for minutes.

events.title: Fifty million years from now (a qualitative projection)
events.when: about 50 million years in the future
events.summary: Nobody can map this precisely, but the trends are clear. The Juan de Fuca plate is shrinking and breaking into pieces; most geologists expect subduction here to die out within tens of millions of years, as it already has off California, leaving a San Andreas-style sliding boundary and quieting the Cascade volcanoes. North America will keep drifting west-southwest at a couple of centimetres a year, roughly 1,000 km over 50 million years, carrying Seattle with it, while Baja California and Los Angeles slide north past the coast toward Alaska. Puget Sound, the Olympics and even Mount Rainier are fleeting: in 50 million years they will have been eroded, filled or rebuilt many times over, as the whole 40-million-year life of the Cascade arc has been shorter than this span.
events.at_your_spot: In 50 million years {place} will still be part of North America, but roughly a thousand kilometres to the west-southwest of where it is now, with no Cascade volcanoes left to see from it.
